subtitle: A guide for Singapore records and IT teams

slides.heading: The short answer
slides.body: No storage that stays connected to a network is fully ransomware-proof. CISA recommends offline, encrypted backups of critical data, tested regularly, because ransomware seeks out and encrypts reachable backups.
slides.callout: For long-term records, archival microfilm adds a copy that is offline by nature and cannot be encrypted by malware.

slides.heading: What CISA recommends for backups
items: Keep offline, encrypted backups of critical data.
Test backup availability and integrity regularly in a recovery exercise.
Keep "golden images" of critical systems so they can be rebuilt quickly.
Use immutable cloud storage with caution: it may not meet every compliance requirement, and misconfiguration is costly.

slides.heading: What microfilm does and does not protect
items: It protects records: registers, contracts, drawings and financial records, as human-readable images.
It does not restore systems. Databases, applications and live files still need offline digital backups.
It must be made and stored correctly: ISO 18901 film, processed to ISO 18917, stored to ISO 18911.
It needs physical security: a controlled vault, ideally with a duplicate at a second site.

slides.heading: A layered plan for long-term records
steps: on your systems for daily access
for records that must survive any digital failure

slides.heading: Common questions
items: Only storage that is offline and cannot be rewritten is beyond ransomware's reach.
No. Microfilm preserves records. Offline digital backups restore systems and live data.
How does digital data get onto microfilm?
A COM system, or archive writer, writes digital images onto 16 mm or 35 mm film.
